network.overall_strategy: Construct a target-focused network with ten distinct route variants: four experimentally reported discharge feedstocks, acetone-based cyanosulfidic homologation, two alternative Strecker entry sequences from supplied 3-methylbutanal, and three demonstrated metal-catalysed aminations of supplied alpha-ketoisocaproate. These are not ten independent reaction mechanisms or ten demonstrated end-to-end geochemical syntheses. Discharge nodes are explicitly coarse-grained, atom-balanced projections of leucine-producing systems after hydrolysis, not elementary reactions or complete product inventories. Cyanosulfidic homologations likewise combine several experimentally studied operations; S8 represents a formal oxidized-sulfur sink rather than a measured exclusive product. The proposed mild environmental hydrolysis stages remain unvalidated for the leucine aminonitrile. Alpha-ketoisocaproate is an explicit external starting inventory: no unsupported synthesis from isovalerate is inserted. Metal-amination branches use separate, sulfide-poor starting solutions and do not assume transport from the photochemical branch. Neutral formulas represent acid-base families; actual protonation is specified in conditions. All routes are anoxic. Formation environments in molecule records are representative; reaction records specify alternative settings. Terminal coproducts use the schema's intermediate role.

reactions.name: Methane-discharge leucine production: coarse-grained hydrolysed endpoint

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K aqueous trap; electrical-discharge channels are transiently much hotter
conditions.pressure: Approximately 0.5 atm initial gas charge in the cited methane experiment
conditions.other: Anoxic electrical discharge over an aqueous trap. Reported methane-run conditions include 300 torr CH4, 80 torr N2, 0.1 torr NH3 and 0.05 M NH4Cl at pH 8.7. N2 is an atmospheric component; this target-channel projection uses the aqueous ammonia inventory for nitrogen bookkeeping. A proposed environmental implementation would discharge for 1-7 days, then acidify captured precursors to pH 1-2 at 350-370 K and monitor hydrolysis for 1-30 days. These residence-time windows and the mild hydrolysis stage are design assumptions, not reproduced experimental protocols.

reactions.mechanism: Discharge-generated carbon and nitrogen intermediates undergo branched-skeleton assembly, aqueous aminonitrile chemistry and hydrolysis. The atom-balanced target-channel projection is 6 CH4 + NH3 + 2 H2O -> leucine + 9 H2; the actual experiment produces a complex mixture.
reactions.reasoning: Leucine was detected in methane-discharge experiments, at approximately 1.4-7.6 molecules per 100 glycine in the reported runs (Ring et al., 1972; Ring and Miller, 1984). This supports the coarse-grained experimental outcome, not a selective methane-to-leucine mechanism or the displayed hydrogen yield. Detection after analytical hydrolysis does not establish the proposed mild natural workup, which remains speculative. Locally reducing gases, low carbon yield and competition with other C6 amino-acid isomers are major limitations.

reactions.name: Isobutane-discharge leucine production: branched-feedstock variant

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K aqueous trap; transient hot discharge channels
conditions.other: Anoxic isobutane-containing discharge atmosphere with an ammonia-containing aqueous trap. Proposed capture pH 8-9 and discharge screening time 1-7 days. Subsequent environmental hydrolysis would require acidification to pH 1-2, heating to 350-370 K and conversion monitoring over 1-30 days. Exact gas ratios and residence times for this published feedstock run are not given in the supplied report; these operating windows are proposals.

reactions.mechanism: Electrical fragmentation and recombination of a branched hydrocarbon supply a mixed carbonyl/nitrile inventory, followed by aqueous amino-acid precursor formation and hydrolysis. Balanced projection: 3 C4H10 + 2 NH3 + 4 H2O -> 2 leucine + 9 H2.
reactions.reasoning: An isobutane discharge produced leucine at about 6.7 per 100 glycine (Ring and Miller, 1984). The branched feedstock is therefore evidence-based, although retention of its branching in a particular molecular sequence was not established. Its natural abundance and the environmental hydrolysis implementation remain uncertain. The balanced projection is not a claim of selective conversion or a complete gas-product balance.

reactions.name: Acetylene-discharge leucine production: unsaturated-feedstock variant

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K aqueous trap; transient hot discharge channels
conditions.other: Anoxic acetylene-containing discharge with ammonia available in the aqueous trap. Proposed pH 8-9 during capture and 1-7 days of discharge. Acidification to pH 1-2 at 350-370 K is a proposed subsequent environmental hydrolysis stage, monitored over 1-30 days. These are screening conditions, not a transcription of the original acetylene-run protocol.

reactions.mechanism: Discharge-driven addition, fragmentation and recombination generate mixed branched precursors that yield amino acids after aqueous processing. Balanced target-channel projection: 3 C2H2 + NH3 + 2 H2O -> leucine. This balance requires no net hydrogen coproduct.
reactions.reasoning: The acetylene experiment gave approximately 14 leucine per 100 glycine, providing direct evidence for this feedstock variant (Ring and Miller, 1984). That glycine-normalized value is not an absolute carbon yield. Neither selective C6 skeleton formation nor mild environmental hydrolysis was demonstrated; the latter remains an explicit extrapolation.

reactions.name: Propane-discharge leucine production: unbranched-feedstock variant

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K aqueous trap; transient hot discharge channels
conditions.other: Anoxic propane-containing discharge with an ammonia-containing trap, proposed capture pH 8-9 and exposure window 1-7 days. A natural hydrolysis extension would require subsequent acidic heating at pH 1-2 and 350-370 K; monitoring for 1-30 days is proposed rather than validated. Original run-specific pressures and residence times are unavailable in the supplied report.

reactions.mechanism: Radical fragmentation and recombination must create branching before amino-acid precursor formation and hydrolysis. Balanced projection: 2 C3H8 + NH3 + 2 H2O -> leucine + 5 H2.
reactions.reasoning: Leucine was reported from propane discharge at approximately 0.47 per 100 glycine, substantially below several alternative gas feeds (Ring and Miller, 1984). This is retained as an experimentally grounded, low-efficiency alternative, not promoted as a favorable route. The precise skeleton-building mechanism and the proposed mild environmental hydrolysis are unresolved.

reactions.name: Acetone cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: Anoxic aqueous acetone and HCN/CN- pool; proposed pH 8-9. Minimize HCN volatilization and initially shield from irradiation. Allow equilibration before the reductive stage; monitor over hours rather than assuming quantitative cyanohydrin formation. Ammonia addition is deferred.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanide addition to the acetone carbonyl followed by proton transfer forms acetone cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: Acetone cyanohydrin is the established entry to the branched amino-acid branch of the cyanosulfidic network (Patel et al., 2015; Green, Xu and Sutherland, 2021). Subsequent consumption can pull an unfavorable equilibrium forward. The stated pH and temperature are a proposed environmental window, not a verified leucine-optimized protocol.

reactions.name: First cyanosulfidic homologation to isobutyraldehyde cyanohydrin

conditions.other: Anoxic UV-illuminated water; 254 nm is the laboratory irradiation benchmark. H2S/HS- supplies reducing equivalents and sulfur chemistry; HCN is replenished for carbon capture. Proposed pH 6.5-8 with phosphate buffering. Irradiation and reagent additions must be staged and monitored over hours to days; no validated natural-flux residence time is assigned. Copper precipitation and sulfide loss require measurement.

reactions.mechanism: Coarse-grained sulfur-assisted photoreduction, deoxygenation and hydrolysis generate the C4 aldehyde level, followed by HCN capture. Balanced formal redox projection: 4 acetone cyanohydrin + 4 HCN + 8 H2S -> 4 isobutyraldehyde cyanohydrin + 4 NH3 + S8.
reactions.reasoning: This skeleton progression is supported by the acetone branch of Patel et al. (2015), reviewed by Green, Xu and Sutherland (2021). The node combines multiple operations and is not an elementary reaction. S8 is a formal electron-balanced oxidized-sulfur endpoint; actual sulfur speciation may include polysulfides and other species. Sulfidic-anion availability, realistic UV rates and copper speciation constrain geological implementation (Ranjan et al., 2018; Rimmer et al., 2021).

reactions.name: Second cyanosulfidic homologation to isovaleraldehyde cyanohydrin

conditions.other: Anoxic, staged sulfide addition and UV irradiation, with 254 nm as the laboratory benchmark. Proposed pH 6.5-8. Resupply HCN after the relevant reduction/hydrolysis operations; defer deliberate ammonia addition. Monitor intermediate conversion over hours to days rather than assigning an unsupported complete-cascade yield or natural residence time.

reactions.mechanism: A further sulfur-assisted reductive sequence, including thioamide-level chemistry, generates the C5 aldehyde level; HCN capture supplies the sixth carbon. Balanced formal projection: 4 isobutyraldehyde cyanohydrin + 4 HCN + 8 H2S -> 4 isovaleraldehyde cyanohydrin + 4 NH3 + S8.
reactions.reasoning: The second homologation leading to the leucine precursor is described by Patel et al. (2015) and Green, Xu and Sutherland (2021). This is a key skeleton-building bottleneck because several sequential transformations and reagent changes are required. A complete acetone-to-leucine yield was not established in the supplied research. The formal sulfur sink does not establish actual sulfur-product selectivity.

reactions.name: Ammonia conversion of the C6 cyanohydrin to leucine aminonitrile

conditions.other: After the homologation operations, stop deliberate irradiation and introduce ammonia. Proposed pH 8-9 with ammonia at least comparable to residual cyanide; monitor over hours to days. Do not assume compatibility with simultaneous uninterrupted photoreduction. Avoid prolonged heating before hydrolysis.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanohydrin dissociation, aldehyde-ammonia imine formation and cyanide capture replace the hydroxy functionality by an amino group in the net reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Addition of ammonia to the appropriate cyanohydrin furnishes the leucine alpha-aminonitrile in the cyanosulfidic scheme (Patel et al., 2015; Green, Xu and Sutherland, 2021). This aminonitrile, not free leucine, is the cited experimental endpoint. Ammonia availability and diversion toward hydroxy-acid precursors remain important constraints.

reactions.name: Acid-catalysed hydration of leucine aminonitrile to leucinamide
agents: Aqueous H+ from acidic volcanic condensate

conditions.other: Proposed pH 1-2 after acidification by anoxic HCl-rich volcanic condensate; shield from UV. Track nitrile disappearance, amide accumulation and degradation over a proposed 1-30 day screening interval. This interval is not an established completion time. Residual cyanide must be assessed because acidification volatilizes HCN.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile protonation and water addition give an imidic intermediate that tautomerizes to the amide. This is the first chemical stage of nitrile hydrolysis, not necessarily a separately isolated preparation.
reactions.reasoning: Aminonitrile hydrolysis is the conventional completion of Strecker chemistry (Miller, 1957), but the supplied research does not establish leucine-aminonitrile hydration kinetics under these mild environmental conditions. This environmental implementation is explicitly speculative. Patel et al. (2015) do not validate this extension. Strong-acid analytical hydrolysis cannot be treated as proof that the same conversion occurs efficiently in a natural pool.

reactions.name: Leucinamide hydrolysis to leucine
agents: Aqueous H+ from acidic volcanic condensate

conditions.other: Continue the same darkened acidic aqueous stage at proposed pH 1-2; no transfer to a deep hydrothermal vent is required. Monitor leucine formation and destruction over 1-30 days without assuming completion. Released ammonia is predominantly ammonium at this pH.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-catalysed water addition to the amide carbonyl followed by C-N cleavage releases leucine and ammonia/ammonium.
reactions.reasoning: This is standard amide hydrolysis within the Strecker completion sequence (Miller, 1957). However, the proposed pH-temperature-time implementation is speculative because substrate-specific conversion and survival data are absent from the supplied research. It is a shared downstream uncertainty for the explicit aminonitrile pathways, not an independently demonstrated cyanosulfidic leucine synthesis. Avoiding prolonged high-temperature vent exposure addresses, but does not eliminate, degradation concerns (Aubrey, Cleaves and Bada, 2009).

reactions.name: Direct three-component Strecker formation of leucine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic aqueous 3-methylbutanal, ammonia and HCN/CN-. Proposed pH 8-9, ammonia at least comparable to cyanide, and hours-to-days monitoring. Protect the volatile aldehyde and HCN from excessive loss. Add ammonia before or together with cyanide rather than deliberately accumulating the cyanohydrin first.

reactions.mechanism: Aldehyde-ammonia condensation produces an imine/iminium species, followed by cyanide addition to generate the racemic alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: The required aldehyde identity and reaction class follow established Strecker chemistry and the interpretation of discharge amino-acid synthesis (Miller, 1957; Ring et al., 1972). The supplied research does not provide a substrate-specific optimum for this isolated preparation; the operating window is an extrapolation. Supplying 3-methylbutanal makes the carbon-skeleton boundary explicit rather than claiming selective formation from C1 gases.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin-first Strecker entry from supplied isovaleraldehyde

conditions.other: Anoxic aqueous aldehyde and HCN/CN-, proposed pH 8-9. Initially omit deliberate ammonia addition so the cyanohydrin can accumulate; assess equilibration over hours. Subsequently use rxn_008 rather than assuming a distinct direct substitution mechanism.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible nucleophilic cyanide addition to 3-methylbutanal produces its cyanohydrin without changing the existing branched carbon skeleton.
reactions.reasoning: The downstream cyanohydrin and its conversion to leucine aminonitrile are supported by Patel et al. (2015). Direct entry from externally supplied aldehyde is standard carbonyl chemistry but is not documented as a separate leucine preparation in the supplied report; its standalone environmental implementation is therefore speculative. This pathway differs by reagent ordering and intermediate accumulation, not by an independent ultimate Strecker mechanism.

reactions.name: Nickel-catalysed reductive amination of supplied alpha-ketoisocaproate
agents: Metallic Ni supported on SiO2-Al2O3, laboratory catalyst formulation

conditions.temperature: 295 K, corresponding to the reported 22 degrees Celsius
conditions.other: Abiotic aqueous mineral-interface batch: 30 mM keto acid, five equivalents NH4HCO3 corresponding to 150 mM total ammonia/ammonium, pH 8, 72 hours, anoxic. Use an initially sulfide-poor and cyanide-poor solution. Geological translation requires a cool H2-fed confined pore and an accessible unpassivated Ni surface; the supported laboratory formulation is not assumed to be a naturally occurring mineral.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia-carbonyl condensation followed by metal-mediated activation of H2 and reduction of the imine produces leucine; competing carbonyl hydrogenation is represented by rxn_016.
reactions.reasoning: Conversion of alpha-ketoisocaproate to leucine over Ni is directly supported (Kaur et al., 2024). The reported yield ranges span several substrates and are not assigned here as a leucine-specific yield. The 6 mM ammonia result for alanine is not extrapolated to leucine. This is a demonstrated supplied-precursor conversion, not a solution to the unresolved prebiotic origin of alpha-ketoisocaproate. Sulfide carryover is avoided by not coupling this branch to the photochemical solution.

reactions.name: Iron-meteorite-catalysed reductive amination of supplied alpha-ketoisocaproate
agents: Ground Aletai iron meteorite with accessible metallic Fe-Ni surfaces

conditions.catalyst: Ground Aletai iron meteorite, reported loading corresponding to 18 mol% Ni
conditions.other: Abiotic aqueous batch: 30 mM keto acid, 150 mM total ammonia/ammonium supplied as NH4HCO3, pH 8, 72 hours, anoxic. Freshly exposed metallic surface is required for comparison with the experiment. Do not substitute an unspecified weathered meteorite or sulfide-coated grain without measuring activity.

reactions.mechanism: Accessible meteoritic metal sites activate hydrogen and reduce the ammonia-derived imine; carbonyl reduction competes.
reactions.reasoning: Ground iron meteorite catalysis of the supplied keto-acid-to-amino-acid conversion is supported by Kaur et al. (2024), including leucine among the tested products. Meteoritic metal offers a geochemical source of Ni, but grinding, exposed surface area, weathering and passivation are consequential boundary conditions. No upstream keto-acid synthesis is implied, and the competing hydroxy-acid outcome is retained.

reactions.name: Palladium-catalysed reductive amination benchmark
agents: Palladium on carbon, laboratory benchmark formulation

conditions.other: Abiotic aqueous batch: 30 mM keto acid, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, 72 hours, anoxic. Use a sulfide-poor and cyanide-poor starting solution. This is an experimental catalytic comparator; a naturally abundant equivalent of Pd/C is not assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Pd activates H2 and preferentially hydrogenates the imine formed from the keto acid and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated leucine formation from its keto acid using Pd/C. Across the tested substrates, Pd favored amino acids over hydroxy acids more strongly than Ni, but the supplied report does not establish a leucine-specific yield or selectivity. Palladium rarity and catalyst formulation limit geochemical extrapolation. This route is included for experimental support, not presented as equally geologically available to meteoritic Fe-Ni.

reactions.name: Competing nickel-mediated reduction to alpha-hydroxyisocaproate
agents: Ni-bearing surface supplied either by Ni/SiO2-Al2O3 or by accessible meteoritic Fe-Ni metal

conditions.catalyst: Alternative Ni-bearing catalyst preparations, not a required catalyst mixture
conditions.other: Parallel reaction under the pH 8, 72-hour conditions of rxn_013 or rxn_014, including the ammonia-containing medium. Quantify both amino acid and hydroxy acid rather than equating keto-acid disappearance with leucine yield.

reactions.mechanism: Metal-mediated hydrogenation reduces the keto-acid carbonyl directly to an alcohol without nitrogen incorporation.
reactions.reasoning: Hydroxy-acid formation competes with reductive amination in the Ni and meteorite experiments (Kaur et al., 2024). The roughly comparable amino-/hydroxy-acid production reported across those experiments must not be treated as a measured leucine-specific 1:1 ratio. This is a connected competing sink, not an additional pathway to leucine.

pathways.name: Methane-discharge route
pathways.description: Experimentally observed leucine-producing discharge system represented by one coarse-grained node. The natural acidic hydrolysis implementation is conditional; the node does not establish a selective elementary methane-to-leucine reaction.

pathways.name: Isobutane-discharge route
pathways.description: An experimentally reported branched-hydrocarbon feedstock variant. Its distinctness is the starting gas inventory, not a demonstrated independent downstream amino-acid mechanism.

pathways.name: Acetylene-discharge route
pathways.description: An experimentally reported unsaturated-feedstock variant producing leucine in a complex hydrolysed mixture. The glycine-normalized abundance is not an absolute synthesis yield.

pathways.name: Propane-discharge route
pathways.description: An experimentally reported but comparatively inefficient feedstock variant requiring branching to emerge during discharge chemistry. Natural hydrolysis remains conditional.

pathways.name: Acetone-based cyanosulfidic route with conditional hydrolysis
pathways.description: Sequential cyanohydrin formation and two reductive homologations build the branched skeleton, followed by ammonia conversion to the demonstrated leucine aminonitrile endpoint. The final two hydrolysis nodes are chemically grounded environmental extrapolations, not a reported integrated acetone-to-leucine preparation.

pathways.name: Direct Strecker entry from supplied isovaleraldehyde
pathways.description: Supplied 3-methylbutanal reacts with ammonia and cyanide without deliberate cyanohydrin accumulation. Completion to leucine depends on validating the shared mild hydrolysis stages; this pathway does not provide the aldehyde's upstream synthesis.

pathways.name: Cyanohydrin-first Strecker entry from supplied isovaleraldehyde
pathways.description: Capture supplied aldehyde as its cyanohydrin before ammonia addition. This is a distinct reagent-order and intermediate-entry variant, not an independent ultimate Strecker mechanism. It shares the same unvalidated mild hydrolysis completion as P5 and P6.

pathways.name: Supported-nickel amination of supplied alpha-ketoisocaproate
pathways.description: Demonstrated terminal conversion using H2, ammonia and supported Ni. Alpha-ketoisocaproate is an explicit starting inventory with unresolved prebiotic provenance. Rxn_016 competes but is not part of the leucine-producing sequence.

pathways.name: Meteoritic Fe-Ni amination of supplied alpha-ketoisocaproate
pathways.description: Demonstrated terminal conversion with ground iron meteorite under specified hydrogenation conditions. Accessible metallic surface and precursor supply are required; an unspecified weathered meteorite is not an equivalent catalyst.

pathways.name: Palladium benchmark amination of supplied alpha-ketoisocaproate
pathways.description: Experimentally supported terminal amination serving as a selectivity benchmark. It does not resolve the keto-acid source, palladium scarcity or availability of a natural catalyst equivalent to Pd/C.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ring et al. (1972) and Ring & Miller (1984) support leucine production in methane-discharge systems. The explicitly coarse-grained, post-hydrolysis interpretation is acceptable, and the supplied balance check establishes conservation. This supports a laboratory endpoint, not selective methane-to-leucine conversion or environmentally demonstrated hydrolysis. The displayed reaction record lacks the quantitative discharge and workup conditions needed for stronger environmental confidence.
suggestions: Attach the experimental gas composition, aqueous composition, discharge duration and hydrolysis protocol to rxn_001.
Report leucine yield and isomer distribution separately from the formal stoichiometric projection.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ring & Miller (1984) support the isobutane-discharge variant, reporting approximately 6.7 leucine molecules per 100 glycine molecules. That ratio establishes detection, not absolute feedstock conversion. The balanced endpoint projection is valid within its declared scope; environmental realization still requires specification of the discharge setting and post-discharge hydrolysis.
suggestions: Link rxn_002 to the specific isobutane experiment and its complete preparation and workup conditions.
Keep glycine-normalized abundance distinct from absolute leucine yield and selectivity.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The acetylene-discharge endpoint is supported by Ring & Miller (1984), with approximately 14 leucine molecules per 100 glycine molecules. The supplied balance check confirms that rxn_003 conserves atoms without requiring an additional coproduct. Nevertheless, the projected equation is not an elementary mechanism or a complete experimental product inventory. Environmental confidence is limited by unspecified discharge and hydrolysis conditions.
suggestions: Specify the acetylene-containing gas mixture, electrical energy input, aqueous trapping conditions and hydrolysis workup.
Retain the coarse-grained annotation and avoid interpreting the equation as quantitative conversion.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ring & Miller (1984) support leucine detection from propane-discharge experiments, at approximately 0.47 leucine molecules per 100 glycine molecules. The low abundance limits productivity claims but does not invalidate target formation. The declared coarse-grained endpoint conserves atoms. As with the other discharge variants, laboratory hydrolysis must be distinguished from demonstrated environmental release of free leucine.
suggestions: Document the specific propane experiment, including analytical identification and hydrolysis conditions.
Quantify absolute leucine recovery and competing amino-acid isomers without treating low yield as absence of synthesis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Patel et al. (2015), as summarized in the supplied research, support the acetone-derived sequence through the leucine aminonitrile. The homologations are acceptable as declared multistage modules, and S8 is explicitly a formal sulfur sink rather than an asserted exclusive product. The principal unresolved extension is rxn_009 followed by rxn_010 under mild environmental conditions: standard nitrile and amide hydrolysis chemistry does not establish adequate rates, substrate survival or leucine recovery under those unspecified conditions. The network appropriately acknowledges this limitation.
suggestions: Attach the experimentally supported staged operations, reagent concentrations, Cu speciation and UV exposure to rxn_006 and rxn_007.
Measure leucine aminonitrile hydration and leucinamide hydrolysis at explicitly specified pH, temperature and residence time, including competing decomposition.
Justify the transition from ammonia-containing synthesis conditions to acidic hydrolysis, or use a demonstrated laboratory workup while limiting the environmental claim.
Keep sulfur stoichiometry identified as formal bookkeeping unless product speciation is measured.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Supplied 3-methylbutanal is the correct aldehyde for a leucine Strecker synthesis, and rxn_011 has sound net chemistry. Treating the aldehyde as an external starting inventory is legitimate and does not create a missing reaction. The route remains conditional at the proposed mild hydrolysis stages, particularly leucinamide-to-leucine conversion. Appropriate ammonia/cyanide concentrations and pH are also needed to establish aminonitrile formation rather than persistent cyanohydrin accumulation.
suggestions: Provide substrate-specific Strecker conditions and quantify aminonitrile formation versus cyanohydrin and other products.
Validate rxn_009 and rxn_010 under the intended environmental conditions, or explicitly substitute a demonstrated hydrolysis workup.
Specify acid supply, pH adjustment and precursor retention during the hydrolysis stage.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cyanohydrin formation from supplied isovaleraldehyde is chemically reasonable, and the supplied Patel et al. (2015) account supports ammonia conversion of the corresponding cyanohydrin to the leucine aminonitrile. This conversion is consistent with coupled carbonyl, imine and cyanide equilibria rather than requiring direct substitution of hydroxide. The route is coherent but shares the same unvalidated mild hydrolysis endpoint as P5 and P6.
suggestions: Specify the conditions that shift the cyanohydrin/aminonitrile equilibria toward mol_016 and measure its recovery.
Demonstrate both hydrolysis stages at the proposed pH, temperature and duration.
Keep this route identified as an alternative Strecker entry sequence, not independent evidence for the shared hydrolysis steps.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) directly support nickel-catalysed reductive amination of supplied alpha-ketoisocaproate to leucine. The external ketoacid inventory is an accepted starting assumption. Including rxn_016 correctly recognizes competing carbonyl reduction; it is scored here as an associated side branch, not a step toward leucine. Separate sulfide-poor solutions avoid an unsupported transfer from the photochemical branch. Environmental realization of the supported catalyst and pressurized H2 supply remains less established than the laboratory chemistry.
suggestions: Attach the reported reference conditions: 22 degrees C, pH 8, 5 bar H2, 72 hours, 30 mM ketoacid and five equivalents of NH4HCO3, together with catalyst loading and preparation.
Provide leucine-specific yield and aminoacid/hydroxyacid selectivity; do not transfer pooled substrate yields or the low-ammonia alanine result to leucine.
Describe the physical H2 reservoir and distinguish the demonstrated supported catalyst from any proposed natural analogue.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied Kaur et al. (2024) research directly supports leucine formation using ground iron meteorite, H2 and an ammonium source. Testing an actual meteoritic catalyst gives this branch a comparatively strong environmental anchor, although grinding, surface accessibility, sustained H2 pressure and solution composition still require physical justification. The declared external ketoacid supply is not a pathway defect. Hydroxyacid competition should be quantified specifically for this substrate and catalyst.
suggestions: Specify meteorite identity, particle size, catalyst loading, surface preparation and the complete experimental solution conditions.
Explain how the setting maintains the required H2 pressure and accessible, sufficiently active metal surfaces.
Report leucine-specific selectivity and represent the meteorite-mediated route to mol_020 if supported by the substrate-specific measurements.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) support palladium-catalysed leucine production from alpha-ketoisocaproate. Identifying this branch as a benchmark correctly separates demonstrated laboratory chemistry from a geochemical synthesis claim. The reaction itself is strong, but the displayed environment does not establish an accessible natural equivalent of Pd/C or the required H2 supply. The study-wide yield and selectivity ranges should not be presented as leucine-specific measurements.
suggestions: Retain the benchmark designation and attach the Pd/C loading and full experimental protocol.
Provide the leucine-specific conversion, yield and selectivity from the primary data.
If making an environmental claim, document accessible Pd-bearing catalytic material and the required physical conditions rather than assuming laboratory Pd/C is naturally supplied.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally valid: all 20 molecule nodes and 16 reaction nodes participate in a connected graph, IDs are consistent, and the authoritative balance check reports no atom or charge violations. The inferred coefficients are reasonable; S8 normalization is not evidence of mis-specification. Terminal sulfur and hydroxyacid products are legitimate endpoints. Literature alignment is strong for the discharge endpoints, the cyanosulfidic aminonitrile sequence and the three metal-catalysed aminations. Racemic leucine satisfies the stated target. External aldehyde and ketoacid inventories are accepted as declared, and neither route count nor shared intermediates earns additional confidence. P1-P4 and P8-P10 support actual leucine production under experimental conditions, whereas P5-P7 remain conditional on rxn_009 and rxn_010 under the proposed mild conditions. The displayed records lack quantitative reaction conditions and reaction-linked citations despite the introductory statements about such records. Environmental confidence therefore remains limited, especially for hydrolysis, staged photochemistry and supported-metal catalyst realization. No photochemical-to-metal transfer is assumed or required. Overall, this is a credible, appropriately qualified synthesis network, but its unresolved implementation and hydrolysis evidence keep complete-network confidence below the 0.90 approval threshold.
